gloss_terse: to hamstring (an animal), cut the leg tendons of horses or oxen, rendering them useless
gloss_readable: A Piel denominative verb derived from a root meaning 'sinew' or 'tendon,' used exclusively for the act of hamstringing animals — slashing the tendons of horses or oxen to cripple them. In wartime contexts (Josh 11:6, 9; 2 Sam 8:4), God commands or David performs this on captured chariot horses, ensuring Israel does not rely on military cavalry. In Gen 49:6, Jacob's rebuke of Simeon and Levi recalls their wanton destruction: 'they hamstrung an ox.' Spanish 'desjarretar' and English 'hamstring' consistently reflect this specific act of disabling by severing leg sinews.

senses.1: To hamstring, i.e., sever the leg tendons of an animal (especially horses or oxen) so as to permanently cripple it. Used in military contexts where captured chariot horses are rendered useless at divine command (Josh 11:6, 9; 2 Sam 8:4 = 1 Chr 18:4), and once of wanton violence against livestock (Gen 49:6). Spanish 'desjarretarás' and French calques confirm the specificity of this act across translations.

gloss_terse: to twist, make crooked, pervert; to distort what is straight or right
gloss_readable: Rooted in the idea of physical twisting, this verb extends powerfully into moral and judicial territory. In its Piel stem it describes the deliberate distortion of paths, justice, or conduct — the leaders of Micah 3:9 'make crooked all that is straight,' and in Isa 59:8 the wicked 'have twisted their paths.' The Niphal participle in Prov 28:18 describes one who is 'crooked in ways,' while the Hiphil in Job 9:20 has God declaring a person perverse. Spanish 'torcer/torcieron' and German equivalents preserve the core image of bending what should be straight.

senses.1: To twist, make crooked, or pervert — used of moral and behavioral distortion. The Piel describes deliberate warping of paths or justice (Isa 59:8 'their paths they have twisted'; Mic 3:9 'all that is straight they make crooked'). The Niphal portrays a settled state of crookedness in conduct (Prov 28:18 'crooked in ways'; Prov 10:9). The Hiphil in Job 9:20 uniquely has God as subject: 'he would declare me perverse.' Spanish 'tuercen' and 'torcieron' preserve the physical twisting metaphor applied to moral reality.

gloss_terse: poplar or willow tree (populus Euphratica), a water-loving tree found near streams
gloss_readable: A noun designating the poplar or willow (populus Euphratica), a tree that flourishes along watercourses. In Lev 23:40, branches of willows of the brook are gathered for the Feast of Tabernacles. The famous Ps 137:2 pictures the exiles hanging their harps 'upon the willows' by the rivers of Babylon. In Isa 44:4, the righteous spring up 'like willows by streams of water.' Spanish 'sauces' and French 'saules' (willows) consistently identify this as a riparian tree species, while Job 40:22 places it in the habitat of Behemoth.

senses.1: A poplar or willow tree (populus Euphratica), characteristically growing beside streams and watercourses. Featured in the Feast of Tabernacles liturgy as 'willows of the brook' (Lev 23:40), in the iconic lament of exile where harps hang on willows by Babylon's rivers (Ps 137:2), and as a simile for flourishing growth in Isa 44:4. Spanish 'sauces,' French branches, and English 'willows' uniformly identify this water-loving tree. Isa 15:7's 'Wadi of the Willows' uses it as a place name in Moab.

gloss_terse: to be shrewd, crafty, or prudent; to act with cunning or discernment
gloss_readable: A verb spanning the morally ambiguous territory between wisdom and cunning. In 1 Sam 23:22, Saul warns that David 'is exceedingly crafty' — here the word carries a negative, threatening sense. Yet in Proverbs, the same root takes on positive coloring: the naive 'becomes prudent' through correction (Prov 19:25), and heeding reproof makes one shrewd (Prov 15:5). In Ps 83:3, enemies 'make crafty their counsel' against God's people. Spanish distinguishes 'astuto' (cunning) from 'prudente' (prudent), revealing the dual moral valence that makes this word so contextually rich.

senses.1: To be shrewd or crafty in a negative sense — to act with cunning, guile, or deceptive cleverness. Saul's warning about David in 1 Sam 23:22 ('he is exceedingly crafty') and the enemies' scheming in Ps 83:3 ('they make crafty their counsel') exemplify hostile, manipulative shrewdness. Spanish 'astuto' and French 'rusé' capture this calculating quality.
senses.2: To become prudent or discerning in a positive sense — to gain practical wisdom through instruction or experience. Proverbs uses this root approvingly: a simple person 'becomes prudent' when they witness correction (Prov 19:25), and heeding reproof makes one wise (Prov 15:5). Spanish 'se hace prudente' and German 'Klugheit' reflect the constructive dimension of shrewdness channeled toward good judgment.

gloss_terse: craftiness, cunning, or prudence; shrewdness applied either deceptively or wisely
gloss_readable: The noun form of the root meaning 'to be shrewd,' carrying the same dual moral charge as its verbal counterpart. In Exodus 21:14 it describes lethal premeditation — killing 'with cunning' — and in Josh 9:4 the Gibeonites act 'with craftiness' to deceive Israel. Yet Proverbs reclaims the word positively: wisdom offers 'prudence to the simple' (Prov 1:4), and personified Wisdom declares 'I dwell with prudence' (Prov 8:12). Spanish 'astucia' and German 'Klugheit' split along the same moral axis, revealing how context determines whether this quality is vice or virtue.

senses.1: Craftiness or cunning — shrewd calculation applied deceptively or with harmful intent. In Exod 21:14 it characterizes premeditated murder ('with cunning'), and in Josh 9:4 the Gibeonites employ it to trick Israel into a covenant. Spanish 'con astucia' and French 'avec ruse' emphasize the manipulative, underhanded quality.
senses.2: Prudence or discernment — the same shrewd intelligence channeled constructively toward wise living. Proverbs uses it as a gift of wisdom: 'to give prudence to the simple' (Prov 1:4), and personified Wisdom claims 'I dwell with prudence' (Prov 8:5, 12). German 'Klugheit' (cleverness, prudence) captures this positive sense of practical wisdom.

gloss_terse: herbage, grass; vegetation eaten as fodder by grazing animals
gloss_readable: An Aramaic noun appearing exclusively in Daniel's Aramaic sections, always in the context of Nebuchadnezzar's humiliation. When the king is driven from human society, he eats 'grass like oxen' (Dan 4:25, 32, 33) — his royal diet reduced to field herbage. The word appears in the heavenly decree (Dan 4:15) and again when the judgment is recounted to Belshazzar (Dan 5:21). Spanish 'hierba' and English 'grass' consistently render this as simple field vegetation, underscoring the totality of the king's reduction from palace feasts to animal fodder.

senses.1: Herbage or grass — field vegetation serving as fodder for animals. Used exclusively in the Aramaic sections of Daniel to describe the grass Nebuchadnezzar was condemned to eat like an ox during his period of madness (Dan 4:15, 25, 32, 33; 5:21). Spanish 'hierba,' French and German cognates all render it as simple field grass, emphasizing the king's reduction from royal splendor to bestial existence grazing on common vegetation.

gloss_terse: bough, branch; the spreading limbs of a large tree, used figuratively of empires
gloss_readable: A feminine noun used exclusively in Ezekiel's grand tree allegories, where mighty cedars and vines symbolize empires and kingdoms. In Ezek 17:6 it describes the spreading branches of a vine representing Judah's royal house. The extended cedar allegory of Ezekiel 31 employs it repeatedly: the great tree's boughs grew long (31:5), birds nested in them (31:6), no tree could rival them (31:8), and when the tree falls, its boughs lie broken across mountains and valleys (31:12-13). Spanish 'ramas/ramaje' and English 'boughs/branches' capture the image of grand arboreal limbs that symbolize political reach and power.

senses.1: Boughs or branches of a large tree, used figuratively in prophetic allegory for the extent and splendor of empires. In Ezek 17:6 it describes a vine's spreading branches (Judah's dynasty), while Ezek 31:5-13 deploys it repeatedly for the towering cedar representing Assyria/Egypt — its boughs sheltering nations (v. 6), unrivaled in beauty (v. 8), then shattered in judgment (vv. 12-13). Spanish 'ramas' and 'ramaje' consistently render these as grand spreading limbs.

gloss_terse: Pagiel, son of Ocran; leader of the tribe of Asher during the wilderness period
gloss_readable: A proper name meaning 'encounter of God' or 'God has met,' borne by the appointed leader of the tribe of Asher during the wilderness wanderings. Pagiel son of Ocran appears in the census (Num 1:13), the tribal camp arrangement (Num 2:27), the tabernacle dedication offerings (Num 7:72, 77), and the marching order (Num 10:26). French 'Paguiel' preserves a slightly different vocalization, while Spanish, English, and German consistently render 'Pagiel.'

senses.1: Pagiel ('encounter of God'), son of Ocran, the designated chief of the tribe of Asher during the Israelite wilderness period. He appears exclusively in Numbers in administrative and ceremonial contexts: the census (Num 1:13), camp positioning (Num 2:27), his tabernacle dedication offering on the eleventh day (Num 7:72, 77), and the departure marching order (Num 10:26). French 'Paguiel' reflects an alternate vocalization tradition.

gloss_terse: to separate, set free, release, dismiss; also to escape or slip away
gloss_readable: A verb whose core meaning of separation branches into several vivid applications. David 'slipped away' from Saul's spear (1 Sam 19:10), certain Levites were 'set free' from other duties to devote themselves to music (1 Chr 9:33), and Jehoiada did not 'dismiss' the outgoing priestly divisions during the coup against Athaliah (2 Chr 23:8). In Prov 17:14, whoever 'lets loose' a quarrel is like breaching a dam. The enigmatic Ps 22:7 uses the passive participle in a context of scorn and rejection. Spanish ranges from 'libres' (free) to 'suelta' (release), while French 'glissa au loin' captures the escape sense.

senses.1: To slip away or escape — intransitive separation from danger or a pursuer. In 1 Sam 19:10, David dodges Saul's spear and 'slipped away,' evading death. French 'il glissa au loin' (he slipped far away) vividly captures the motion of narrow escape.
senses.2: To set free, release, or dismiss — transitive liberation from duty or obligation. The Levitical singers in 1 Chr 9:33 were 'free' (released from other service), and Jehoiada strategically did not 'dismiss' the priestly courses during the overthrow of Athaliah (2 Chr 23:8). Spanish 'libres' reflects this sense of formal release.
senses.3: To let loose or unleash — releasing something (especially strife) that then spreads uncontrollably. Prov 17:14 warns that starting a quarrel is like breaching a dam: 'whoever lets loose strife' cannot contain it. Spanish 'el que suelta' (the one who releases) captures the image of deliberate but reckless unleashing. Ps 22:7 may use the passive participle for one 'cast out' or scorned by others.

gloss_terse: Pallu, son of Reuben; ancestor of the Palluites, a Reubenite clan
gloss_readable: A proper name possibly meaning 'distinguished' or 'separated,' borne by the second son of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn. Pallu appears in the genealogical lists tracing Reuben's descendants into Egypt (Gen 46:9), the priestly genealogy (Exod 6:14), the wilderness census and clan registry (Num 26:5, 8), and the Chronicler's tribal record (1 Chr 5:3). He is the ancestor of Eliab and through him of Dathan and Abiram, who later rebelled against Moses. Spanish 'Falú' reflects an alternate phonetic tradition, while French, English, and German consistently use 'Pallu.'

senses.1: Pallu ('distinguished'), second son of Reuben and ancestor of the Palluite clan. He appears in five genealogical registers spanning the patriarchal migration to Egypt (Gen 46:9), the priestly lineage (Exod 6:14), the wilderness census (Num 26:5, 8), and the tribal chronicle (1 Chr 5:3). Notably, his line produces Dathan and Abiram of Korah's rebellion (Num 26:8-9). Spanish 'Falú' preserves a distinctive phonetic rendering.
